newsitem.title: USA: USDA pegs 1996/97 cotton crop at 18.594 mln bales.
newsitem.headline: USDA pegs 1996/97 cotton crop at 18.594 mln bales.

text.p: NYCE cotton prices are likely to trade lower Tuesday in reaction to the the U.S. Department of Agriculture's estimate of 18.594 million bales for the 1996/97 U.S. crop, market sources said.

But while the estimate came in above last month's forecast of 18.159 million 480-lb bales, a strong U.S. production number has already been filtered into the market and prices are not likely to fall the 3.00-cent daily limit.
Tuesday, the most-active December contract hit a fresh contract low of 70.35 cents a lb.
"(The report) has already been figured in to some extent, but lower prices are needed to help shore up the demand side," said David Brandon Jr, an analyst with Smith Barney.
He pegged nearby support in December at 70.00 cents and then at 69.00 cents, the low of the July contract during its delivery period. "Technically, that could be a double bottom," Brandon said.

Higher U.S. supplies boosted ending stocks to 4.9 million bales from 4.5 million bales last month, while domestic use remained unchanged at 11.0 million bales. Imports and exports were also unchanged at 500,000 bales and 5.8 million bales, respectively.

"All of the increase went into ending stocks. The market has to go down to increase exports and bring supply down to manageable level," said Sharon Johnson, an analyst with Frank Schneider and Co Inc.
She said how fast the December contract falls below 70.00 during today's session depends on how willing the trade will be to support prices as they fall.

Increases in the U.S. crop were expected to show up in Texas and the Delta. Indeed, the USDA raised its production forecast to 4.05 million bales from 3.85 million bales in Texas and to 1.8 million from 1.67 million bales in Mississippi.
Internationally, decreases in supply estimates in Pakistan, Brazil and Uzbekistan were offset by increases in India, Australia, West Africa and the U.S., analysts said.
"This is encouragement for all the cotton bears who have pointed all along to oversupplies," Brandon said. "The supply side is crystal clear. Now, we need to look at demand."
